rows.item: Title slide (slide 1): course name, lecturer and semester
rows.note: Course details, not teaching content.

rows.item: Definition (slide 2): terminology is the discipline concerned with the study and compilation of specialised terms; not a new field, but systematically developed in recent decades
rows.where: Words to remember, Chapter 21 (Terminology); Chapter 21, Step 1
rows.note: Shortened to a one-line definition, with a citation to Cabré (1999) added.

rows.item: Social and political aspects and origins (slides 2–4): the need for rules for creating terms as science became international in the 19th century; scientists leading in the 18th and 19th centuries and engineers and technicians in the 20th; naming of concepts in chemistry, botany and zoology; the start of the field in the 1930s
rows.note: History is not needed to use terms well.

rows.item: The three schools and their founders (slides 5–7): Lotte and the Soviet School; the Prague School (based on Saussure); Wüster, an Austrian engineer and industrialist, founder of modern terminology and the Vienna School (1898–1977, with his portrait); technology needing agreement on terms
rows.note: History and schools are not needed to use terms well.

rows.item: Development of the field (slides 8–11): social need; society changing from rural to industrial; the technologisation of society and the value of information; standard language and education; five social changes that affect terminology (new concepts from science and technology, new ways of communicating, mass communication, government intervention, growth of information and databases)
rows.note: Theory beyond a beginner’s level.

rows.item: The four periods of modern terminology (slides 12–15): origins 1930–1960 (Wüster and Lotte); structuring 1960–1975 (computers, first databank, first standardisation); boom 1975–1985 (language planning); expansion 1985–present (computer science, tools, a market for terminology)
rows.note: History is not needed to use terms well.

rows.item: Three approaches of the classical schools (slides 16–18): an interdisciplinary and independent subject (Moscow and Prague); philosophy and concept systems (Vienna); the linguistic side, with terms as part of the lexicon (Prague); terminology theory rests on the first approach
rows.note: Theory beyond a beginner’s level.

rows.item: Functions of terminology and four points of view (slides 19–21): linguists (special languages within the general language), specialists (terms and concepts), users (practical communication units judged by precision, suitability and standardisation), language planners (intervention and modernisation)
rows.note: Theory beyond a beginner’s level.

rows.item: Direct users of terminology (slides 22–23): specialists in each subject field, who define concepts, update terms and keep them in use
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: Intermediary users (slide 23): translators, technical writers and linguists, who need glossaries and specialised dictionaries for technical writing and translating
rows.note: Kept as the idea that translators use glossaries, dictionaries and termbases; technical writers and linguists are not mentioned.

rows.item: Importance of terminology (slide 24): the key to all sciences and fields; enriches language with technical terms that give formality and modernity; linked to translation studies, linguistics, computer science and information technology
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: Working methods (slides 25–27): terminology adapted to the linguistic system (Vienna, Moscow, Prague); translation-oriented terminology (Quebec; UN, EU, UNESCO); terminology for language planning (minority languages)
rows.note: Theory beyond a beginner’s level.

rows.item: Characteristics of the field (slides 28 and 69): deals with concepts to produce terms; a descriptive approach; aims to serve translation and lexicography (slide 28) or language planning (slide 69) and to achieve standardisation
rows.note: Theory beyond a beginner’s level.

rows.item: Translators and terminologists (slide 29): inventing terms is as old as language use; translators provide translations of foreign terms and work with two languages; the terminologist coins new terms and standardises them, and works with one language
rows.where: Chapter 21, Step 2 (both points); Words to remember, Chapter 21 (Terminologist); Try it question 1
rows.note: Corrected: a terminologist works in one or more languages, and the contrast is now whole texts versus the terms of a field.

rows.item: Terminology and translation (slide 30): the two fields are closely related; both use language as target, content and medium
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: Skills of the translator (slide 31): fluency in the source and target languages; encyclopedic knowledge; awareness of the topic; proper experience
rows.note: Rewritten as simple points and merged with similar points from other notes; ‘encyclopedic knowledge’ is not a separate point.

rows.item: Translators as users of terminology and technical translation (slides 32–34): translators mediate between specialists; technical translation is supported by multilingual terminology; a solid background in technical terms; content and form both preserved; large multilingual technical dictionaries
rows.note: Only the point that translators use glossaries and dictionaries is kept (see intermediary users above).

rows.item: When dictionaries and databanks fail, the translator thinks like a terminologist to provide the equivalent (slide 34)
rows.where: Chapter 21, Step 3 (fourth point); Try it question 3
rows.note: Now says to search the client’s guide, UNTERM and Arabterm first, then create an accurate term and record it.

rows.item: Categories of terms by form, part 1 (slide 35): terms formed by affixes or compounds, such as illness and afterburner
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: Initialisms (slide 36): the initials of an organisation, document or process, such as CBC (Complete Blood Count) and CIA (Central Intelligence Agency)
rows.where: Chapter 21, Step 1 (CBC also appears in the term list in Step 4)
rows.note: Now defined by how the letters are read (one by one) instead of by what they stand for.

rows.item: Acronyms (slide 36): words formed from the initial segments of a phrase, such as LASER (Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation)
rows.note: Now defined by how the letters are read (as a word); the long form of LASER is not given.

rows.item: Abbreviations (slide 37): forms that reproduce part of a word and act as its symbol, such as vol (volume) and 3rd (third)
rows.note: Only vol. (volume) was kept.

rows.item: Clippings (slide 37): the first part of a word or phrase, used to make speech economical, such as super (superintendent) and hyper (hyperactive)
rows.note: Only super (superintendent) was kept, and the definition now says ‘often keeping its first part’.

rows.item: Categories of terms by function (slide 38): nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs; terms in special languages are mostly nouns
rows.note: Too theoretical for beginners.

rows.item: Categories of terms by meaning (slide 39): objects (computer monitor), processes (placement test), features (dead language), relationships (collocations)
rows.note: Too theoretical for beginners.

rows.item: Categories of terms by linguistic origin (slides 40–41): derivation and conversion; three kinds of borrowing: from a dead language (cranium, internus), from another living language (internet, Algebra), from other dialects or subject fields (McDonaldization; process data in computer science, application in law)
rows.note: Borrowing is taught instead as a translation procedure (Chapter 13) and a way to make a word (Chapter 17), with other examples.

rows.item: International guidelines for term creation, 1 and 2 (slide 42): create terms systematically (form, syntax, meaning, use); follow the spelling and pronunciation of the language
rows.note: Only the general idea of following the language’s normal rules for making words remains (Chapter 21, Step 3).

rows.item: International guidelines for term creation, 3 and 4 (slides 42–43): a widely accepted term should not be changed without good reasons; a replacement term must be accepted as a full substitute
rows.note: Kept as an instruction (‘do not change an accepted term without a good reason’); the point about full substitutes was left out.

rows.item: Rules for names of terms, first group (slides 44–46): the term relates directly to the concept and expresses it clearly (1); follows the general rules of word-formation (3); is not redundant, such as {{التطرّف الراديكالي}} (4); has no unnecessary information (5); has no homonyms and is not ambiguous (7 and 8)
rows.note: Reduced to one sentence: clear, short, one meaning, normal word-building and no repeating; the {{التطرّف الراديكالي}} example is kept.

rows.item: Rules for names of terms, second group (slides 44–46): lexically systematic (2); no regional variants such as US and UK (6); independent of context (9); the homonym example fine (adjective) and fine (noun)
rows.note: Left out to keep the rules short for beginners.

rows.item: The Arabic academies as the bodies that examine and approve Arabic terms (slides 47, 55 and 57: the Egyptian, Iraqi and Jordanian academies)
rows.where: Chapter 21, Step 2 (paragraph after the two points); Step 3 (third point)
rows.note: Reduced to one sentence naming the academies in Cairo, Baghdad and Amman; Damascus and the Rabat bureau were added.

rows.item: The Arabic Academy in Egypt, ten steps for term lists (slides 47–49): committees examine terms from universities, governments, specialists and individuals; give an Arabic equivalent and define it; circulate the lists; collect members’ opinions; discuss in the weekly council; present at the annual conference; publish in the journal; wait one year for objections from Arab scholars; accepted if there is no veto
rows.note: Too detailed for beginners; only the fact that academies approve terms is kept.

rows.item: General language and special language (slide 50): the differences between them
rows.note: Only the slide title was in the text we have, and the topic is not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: Terminology versus lexicography (slides 51–53)
rows.note: Only the slide title was in the text we have, and the topic is not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: How to translate a term (slide 54): study the term to understand its detailed meaning; study its etymology; find an equivalent that faithfully matches the concept
rows.note: Kept as the first three points, with new examples, the client’s guide, UNTERM and Arabterm added, plus two more points on creating and recording a term.

rows.item: Iraqi Academy of Science, term-formation methods (slides 55–56): specialists examine terms; old Arabic scientific books; consulting scientists, academies and journals; standardising six months after approval; balancing old and new terms; preferring Arabic-sounding to borrowed terms; one Arabic term for each foreign term; avoiding ambiguity
rows.note: Too detailed for beginners; the academy is only named (Baghdad).

rows.item: Jordanian Academy of Arabic, term-formation methods (slide 57): the Arabic term reflects the foreign one and shows its function; the old scientific term is preferred to a new coinage; a common foreign term is kept
rows.note: Too detailed for beginners; the academy is only named (Amman).

rows.item: Terminography (slide 58): a branch of lexicography and terminology dealing with technical and scientific terms; links linguistics, logic and information science
rows.note: Theory beyond a beginner’s level.

rows.item: Technical dictionaries (slide 59): contain the standardised terms of one subject; subject-oriented; the product of terminography
rows.where: Chapter 21, Step 4; Words to remember and Step 3, Chapter 3
rows.note: Renamed ‘specialised dictionary’ and reduced to one line; ‘standardised’ and terminography were dropped.

rows.item: What is a termbase? (slide 60): a database containing terminology and related information, mostly multilingual
rows.where: Words to remember, Chapter 21 (Termbase); Chapter 21, Step 4
rows.note: Shortened to one line; the multilingual point appears as ‘the term in each language’ in Step 4.

rows.item: Termbase entries and fields (slides 61–63): each entry has at least one term; an index field (the term) and a descriptive field with a definition, context or source, subject area, author, creation or modification, and verification status with an ID
rows.note: Reduced to ‘the term in each language, with its definition, field, source and date’; the two field names, author and verification status were left out.

rows.item: Terminology management (slide 64): the technical approach of collecting, processing and presenting terms
rows.where: Words to remember, Chapter 21 (Terminology); Chapter 21, Step 1
rows.note: Not defined on its own; the idea of collecting and managing terms is inside the definition of terminology.

rows.item: Why manage terminology? (slide 65): unmanaged terms become inconsistent, giving confusing translations that cannot be reused and cost more time and resources
rows.note: Shortened to several names for one concept, confused readers and less reuse; the cost in time and resources was left out.

rows.item: Benefits of termbases (slides 66–68): up-to-date data in minutes; easy storage and web access; economy of time and money; spotting redundant terms
rows.note: Cut to one short sentence (‘A team can share and update it’); the benefits in time and money and in spotting mistakes were left out.

rows.item: Goals of termbases (slide 68): translator assistance; standardisation and unification of terms; use of terminography
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level; a similar idea, keeping one term for one idea, appears in Chapter 22, Step 1.

rows.item: Standardisation levels and bodies (slide 70): national, international and regional levels; ISO, ITU and IEC
rows.note: Too specialised for a first handbook.

rows.item: What terminological standardisation is (slides 71–72 and 77–78): agreeing on terms with their definitions; national delegations agreeing on criteria; a choice among competing terms, decided by vote; three factors (economy, appropriateness, precision)
rows.note: Too specialised for a first handbook.

rows.item: ISO (slides 73–75): the name comes from the Greek isos (‘equal’) and is not an acronym; founded in 1947 in place of the national associations that stopped work in the Second World War; headquarters in Geneva; a non-governmental network of over 150 countries; official languages English, French and Russian; technical committees with one member per country; covers everything except electrical work (IEC)
rows.note: Too specialised for a first handbook.

rows.item: First international committee on terminology standardisation (slide 76): created in 1936 at the request of the Soviet Union; names concepts, unifies terms and prepares vocabularies
rows.note: History is not needed to use terms well.

rows.item: How standards are agreed and used (slides 79–81): expert committees, consensus, then a ballot to accept, reject or abstain; standardisation is voluntary but becomes compulsory nationally by decree; international standards appear in several languages, national ones usually in one
rows.note: Too specialised for a first handbook.

rows.item: Types of terminology standards (slide 82): de jure (made by an official body) and de facto (set by market share, such as smartphone, WhatsApp, BBM)
rows.note: Too specialised for a first handbook.

rows.item: Influential factors for the development of terminology translation (slide 83): the status of the language in the country; human resources; translation institutions; supportive legislation; academic research on terminology translation
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: Criticism of dictionaries as a source of Arabic terms (slide 84): poor classification of terms ({{الصنوبر/الرز}}); terms not explained scientifically ({{الحشرة: الدواب الصغار}}); obsolete words
rows.note: Too specialised for a first handbook.

rows.item: Other sources of Arabic terms (slide 85): language books such as {{كتاب النحل والعسل}}; classic science books such as {{كتاب الحاوي في الطب للرازي}} and {{في المنطق إبن سينا}}, which help avoid coining new terms
rows.note: Too specialised for a first handbook.

rows.item: Literal versus sense translation of terms (slide 86): for example conference ({{مؤتمر أو الموازنة}}); literal translation is accepted if it matches the concept
rows.note: Literal and free translation is taught in Chapter 11, with other examples.

rows.item: Affix translation (slide 86): manage – manageable ({{قابل للإدارة}}); anti-biotic ({{مضاد حيوي}})
rows.where: Chapter 17, Step 2 (paragraph after the five methods)
rows.note: The same two examples were kept, spelt manageable and antibiotic, and a third (greenish) was added.

rows.item: Derivation (slide 87): one of the most productive ways to make terms, forming a new word from part of an existing word
rows.note: Kept as ‘derived from an Arabic root’ inside the neologism method.

rows.item: Metaphor defined (slide 87): a figure of speech that uses comparison to make an analogy
rows.note: Chapter 12 defines metaphor in its own words.

rows.item: Two types of metaphor in terms (slide 88): a relationship between the hidden figurative and the literal meaning ({{القصف}}: the sound of thunder or of artillery fire, figuratively); no such relationship ({{عقرب الساعة}})
rows.note: Only the clock example was kept, as {{عقارب الساعة}}, to show that images differ between languages; the two types and {{القصف}} were left out.

rows.item: Three approaches to Arabic terms, the translation approach (slide 89): translating the meaning; sources such as general-purpose dictionaries ({{لسان العرب، تاج العروس، الصحاّح}})
rows.note: Too specialised for a first handbook.

rows.item: Generative approach, derivation (slide 90): {{الكلام المولّد}}; {{استمطار - مطر}} and {{أصيل - أصل}}
rows.note: Only {{الاستمطار}} from {{مطر}} was kept, explained as ‘cloud seeding’; the generative approach is not named.

rows.item: Generative approach, metaphor (slide 90): {{قطار – قافلة الجمال}}
rows.note: Kept as ‘{{قطار}} once meant a line of camels; today it means a train’, without naming the metaphor method.

rows.item: Metaphor-based terms (slide 91): more common in scientific than in administrative bodies, for example throbbing headache and dry cough
rows.note: Only ‘a throbbing headache’ was kept ({{صداع نابض}}), as a shared metaphor that is translated literally; ‘dry cough’ and the comparison with administrative bodies were left out.

rows.item: Borrowing (slide 91): loan words into the target language, such as {{إنترنت، تلفزيون، منجنيق}}
rows.note: The handbook’s examples of borrowing into Arabic (radio, strategy, technology) come from other notes.

rows.item: How to cite references (slide 92): an English format (surname, initial, date, title in italics, city, publisher; example: Baker, In Other Words) and an Arabic format (title in bold; example: {{الأحمد، خالد. (٢٠٢٤). مدخل إلى المصطلح}})
rows.note: The handbook has no citing guide; its References list uses APA style (Baker appears there as the 2018 edition) and gives Arabic sources in transliteration.

rows.item: Definition of terminology: the systematic discipline concerned with studying, compiling and managing specialised terms by analysing concepts to yield clear names
rows.where: Words to remember, Chapter 21 (Terminology); Chapter 21, Step 1
rows.note: Shortened to a plain definition with a citation to Cabré (1999); ‘systematic’ and ‘by analysing concepts’ were dropped, and a second meaning (the set of terms of one field) was added.

rows.item: Historical background: naming in chemistry, botany and zoology in the 18th and 19th centuries, then engineering in the 20th; Wüster and the Vienna School in the 1930s; four periods (Origins 1930–1960, Structuring 1960–1975, Boom 1975–1985, Expansion 1985–present); three schools (Vienna, Moscow, Prague)
rows.note: History and schools are not needed to use terms well.

rows.item: How a translator benefits from terms: translators as intermediary users who rely on terminology, glossaries and specialised dictionaries for technical translation; multilingual terminology keeps both content and form
rows.note: Shortened to one point; keeping content and form was left out.

rows.item: When to act as a terminologist: when dictionaries or databanks give no equivalent, coin and establish an accurate term
rows.where: Chapter 21, Step 3 (fourth point); Try it question 3
rows.note: Now says to search the client’s guide, UNTERM and Arabterm first.

rows.item: Functions of terminology, users’ definition: practical communication units judged by precision, suitability and standardisation
rows.note: Theory beyond a beginner’s level.

rows.item: Functions of terminology, translators’ need for dictionaries and glossaries (translators, technical writers, linguists)
rows.note: Kept for translators only; technical writers and linguists are not named.

rows.item: Functions of terminology, standardisation to help translators: consensus and unification of terms
rows.where: Words to remember, Chapter 21 (Terminologist); Chapter 21, Step 2
rows.note: Reduced to terminologists and academies creating, approving or standardising terms, with the Rabat bureau helping to unify them; consensus is not mentioned.

rows.item: Functions of terminology, changing accepted terms: once a term has gained wide acceptance, it should not be changed without good reasons
rows.note: The same rule, now worded as an instruction.

rows.item: Functions of terminology, importance of terminology management: unmanaged terms become inconsistent, giving confusing definitions and translations that cannot be reused, at a cost in time and resources
rows.note: Shortened; the cost in time and resources was left out.

rows.item: Terminology and translation: the two fields are closely related; both use language as target, content and medium
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: How terminologists work, core role: a terminologist works within one language to coin and standardise terms, unlike a translator, who works across two
rows.where: Words to remember, Chapter 21 (Terminologist); Chapter 21, Step 2 (second point); Try it question 1
rows.note: Corrected: a terminologist works in one or more languages, and the contrast is now whole texts versus the terms of a field.

rows.item: How terminologists work, processing orientations: linguistic system (Vienna, Moscow, Prague); translation-oriented (UN, EU, UNESCO, bilingual regions); language planning (minority or unstable languages)
rows.note: Theory beyond a beginner’s level.

rows.item: How terminologists work, methodology: collecting, processing, presenting and managing terms by morphological, syntactic, semantic and pragmatic rules
rows.where: Words to remember, Chapter 21 (Terminology); Chapter 21, Step 1
rows.note: Only collecting, naming and managing terms is kept, inside the definition of terminology; the rules were left out.

rows.item: Skills of the translator: fluency in both languages; encyclopedic knowledge; awareness of the subject matter; proper translation experience
rows.note: Rewritten as simple points and merged with similar points from other notes; ‘encyclopedic knowledge’ is not a separate point.

rows.item: Skills of the translator, technical background: a solid background in the technical terminology of the field, to preserve content and form
rows.note: Not stated as a skill; Chapter 21 teaches how to find, record and use terms instead.

rows.item: When dictionaries and databanks fail, the translator thinks like a terminologist to provide an accurate technical equivalent
rows.where: Chapter 21, Step 3 (fourth point); Try it question 3
rows.note: Now placed after searching the client’s guide, UNTERM and Arabterm.

rows.item: Categories of terms by form: initialisms (CBC, CIA); acronyms (LASER); abbreviations (vol, 3rd); clippings (super, hyper)
rows.where: Chapter 21, Step 1 (CBC also in the term list in Step 4; LASER in Try it question 2)
rows.note: Definitions simplified around how the letters are read; 3rd and hyper were left out.

rows.item: Categories of terms by meaning: objects (computer monitor), processes (placement test), features (dead language), relationships (collocations)
rows.note: Too theoretical for beginners.

rows.item: Categories of terms by linguistic origin (borrowing): from a dead language (cranium, internus); from another living language (internet, Algebra); from other dialects or subject fields (McDonaldization, process data, application)
rows.note: Borrowing is taught instead as a translation procedure (Chapter 13) and a way to make a word (Chapter 17), with other examples.

rows.item: Rules for names of terms, first group: relates directly to the concept and expresses it clearly; follows the general rules of word-formation; not redundant; no unnecessary information; no homonyms; not ambiguous
rows.note: Reduced to one sentence: clear, short, one meaning and normal word-building; the {{التطرّف الراديكالي}} example comes from her slides.

rows.item: Rules for names of terms, second group: lexically systematic; no morphological variants such as regional US and UK; independent of context
rows.note: Left out to keep the rules short for beginners.

rows.item: Arabic academies ({{مجمع اللغة العربية}}): regional academies as language-planning bodies that coin, examine and standardise specialised Arabic terms
rows.where: Chapter 21, Step 2 (paragraph after the two points)
rows.note: Reduced to one sentence naming the academies in Cairo, Baghdad and Amman; Damascus and the Rabat bureau were added.

rows.item: Egyptian Academy method: committees examine proposed terms; write an Arabic equivalent and a technical definition; circulate lists to members and review them in council; present at the annual conference and publish in the journal; a one-year wait for objections, then the terms are accepted
rows.note: Too detailed for beginners.

rows.item: Iraqi Academy method: specialist review; classical Arabic scientific texts; consulting scientists; Arabic-sounding terms preferred to borrowed ones; standardising six months after approval
rows.note: Too detailed for beginners.

rows.item: Jordanian Academy method: the Arabic equivalent reflects the function of the foreign term; classical scientific terms preferred to new coinages; widely used foreign terms kept
rows.note: Too detailed for beginners.

rows.item: How to translate a term: study the term to understand its detailed meaning; examine its etymology; find an equivalent that faithfully matches the concept
rows.note: Kept as the first three points, with new examples, the client’s guide, UNTERM and Arabterm added, plus two more points on creating and recording a term.

rows.item: Technical dictionaries: contain the standardised terms of one subject and are subject-oriented; the main product of terminography; technical translators rely on multilingual technical dictionaries that cover a large number of terms
rows.where: Chapter 21, Step 4; Words to remember and Step 3, Chapter 3
rows.note: Renamed ‘specialised dictionary’ and reduced to one line; ‘standardised’, terminography and the size of dictionaries were dropped.

rows.item: Termbase, what it is: a database containing terminology and related information, usually multilingual
rows.where: Words to remember, Chapter 21 (Termbase); Chapter 21, Step 4
rows.note: Shortened to one line; the multilingual point appears as ‘the term in each language’ in Step 4.

rows.item: Termbase, organisation: entries with at least one term in the source and target languages; an index field (the term) and a descriptive field (definition, context or source, subject area, author, creation or modification dates, verification status and ID)
rows.note: Reduced to ‘the term in each language, with its definition, field, source and date’; the two field names, author and verification status were left out.

rows.item: Termbase, benefits: updated data in minutes; simple storage with web access; economy of time and money; spotting and removing redundant terms
rows.note: Cut to one short sentence (‘A team can share and update it’).

rows.item: Standardisation bodies, operating levels: national, regional and international
rows.note: Too specialised for a first handbook.

rows.item: Standardisation bodies, ISO, ITU and IEC: ISO founded in 1947 in Geneva, a non-governmental network of national standards institutes from over 150 countries, official languages English, French and Russian, covering everything except electrical and electronic engineering; ITU (listed without a description); IEC, exclusively electrical and electronic standards
rows.note: Too specialised for a first handbook.

rows.item: Types of standards: de jure (official, from recognised bodies) and de facto (set by market share, such as smartphone and WhatsApp)
rows.note: Too specialised for a first handbook.

rows.item: Outline, functions of terminology: the users’ definition (slide 20)
rows.note: Theory beyond a beginner’s level.

rows.item: Outline, functions of terminology: a translator’s need for specialised dictionaries and glossaries; terminology standardises terms and so helps translators
rows.note: Reduced to translators using glossaries, dictionaries and termbases; standardisation is mentioned only through terminologists and academies.

rows.item: Outline, functions of terminology: once a term has gained wide acceptance, it should not be changed without good reasons (slide 42)
rows.note: The same rule, now worded as an instruction.

rows.item: Outline, functions of terminology: why is it important to manage terminology? (slide 65)
rows.note: Shortened to several names for one concept, confused readers and less reuse.

rows.item: Outline, terminology and translation (slide 30)
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: Outline, skills of the translator (slides 30–34)
rows.note: Rewritten as simple points and merged with similar points from other notes.

rows.item: Outline, skills of the translator: when the dictionaries or databanks fail, think like a terminologist to provide the equivalent
rows.where: Chapter 21, Step 3 (fourth point); Try it question 3
rows.note: Now placed after searching the client’s guide, UNTERM and Arabterm.

rows.item: Outline, categories of terms by form: initialisms, acronyms, abbreviations, clippings
rows.note: Kept with simplified definitions and fewer examples.

rows.item: Outline, categories of terms by meaning (objects, processes, features, relationships) and by linguistic origin (three kinds of borrowing)
rows.note: Too theoretical for beginners.

rows.item: Outline, rules for names of terms (slides 44–46)
rows.note: Reduced to one sentence.

rows.item: Outline, how to translate a term (slide 54)
rows.note: Kept as the first three points, with more added.

rows.item: Outline, technical dictionaries (slide 59)
rows.note: Renamed ‘specialised dictionary’ and reduced to one line.

rows.item: Outline, termbase: what it is, how it is organised, and the benefits of termbases (slides 66–68)
rows.where: Words to remember, Chapter 21 (Termbase); Chapter 21, Step 4
rows.note: Kept what a termbase is and holds; the benefits are cut to ‘A team can share and update it’.

rows.item: Idioms 1–5 of her list: put a bug in your ear; Rolling in the aisles; Heard it through the grapevine; Dish the dirt; Be beside yourself
rows.note: Informal, mostly American expressions; Chapter 9 already gives the most common idioms.

rows.item: Idiom 6 of her list: Raining cats and dogs
rows.where: Chapter 9, Steps 1 and 3; Chapter 2 (Your first translation, step by step); Chapter 22, Step 3
rows.note: Also in Samiuallah’s notes and Shaikhah’s slides; the handbook gives Arabic equivalents, which her list did not.

rows.item: Idiom 7 of her list: Stuck their foot in their mouth
rows.note: A common idiom, but Chapter 9 keeps to a short list.

rows.item: Idiom 8 of her list: Spill the beans
rows.where: Chapter 9, Step 3 and Try it; Chapter 14, Step 1
rows.note: Also in Samiuallah’s notes; the handbook gives the Arabic {{أفشى السرّ}}, which her list did not.

rows.item: Idioms 9–14 of her list: Main squeeze (marked ‘slang term’ in her list); Loose lips; Talked my arm off; Nose to the grindstone; Popped a cork; Hot-foot
rows.note: Mostly American slang, and ‘Loose lips’ and ‘Popped a cork’ are unclear on their own.

rows.item: Idioms 15–19 of her list: Watering hole; Tie one on; In two shakes (of a lamb’s tail); Three sheets to the wind; Drunk as a skunk
rows.note: Four of these are about drinking or being drunk and ‘in two shakes’ is informal, so they do not suit this handbook.

rows.item: Idioms 20–24 of her list: Tick someone off; A bull in a china shop; Wipe the floor with someone; Clean someone’s clock; A hole in the wall
rows.note: Informal or American slang, and not needed beside the common idioms in Chapter 9.

rows.item: Idioms 25–29 of her list: Born with a silver spoon in their mouth; Joined at the hip; About to blow off; The whole shooting match; Can’t get my arm around this
rows.note: The first two are common but not needed beside Chapter 9, the third and fifth are unclear as written, and the fourth is American slang.

rows.item: Idioms 30–35 of her list: Walk in the park; A real basket case; A can of worms; Out of whack; Bending my ears; Cock and bull story
rows.note: ‘Walk in the park’ repeats ‘a piece of cake’ (Chapter 9), and the rest are slang, unclear or not needed beside the common idioms.

rows.item: Idioms 36–41 of her list: Make a long story short; One’s heart is in one’s mouth; In a pickle; Flavor of the month; Crying a river; Be toast
rows.note: ‘Make a long story short’ is covered by ‘in a nutshell’ and ‘the long and the short of it’ in Chapter 9, and the rest are informal, American or unclear.

rows.item: Idioms 42–47 of her list: Hustle their bustle; Put lipstick on a pig; Throw someone in the pokey; Wet behind the ears; Feeding someone a line; Swallow something hook, line, and sinker
rows.note: Mostly American slang, and ‘Hustle their bustle’ is unclear as written.

rows.item: Idioms 48–51 of her list: Throw caution to the wind; Lays rubber; Dumper than a stump; Someone is out cold
rows.note: ‘Lays rubber’ is American slang and ‘Dumper than a stump’ is unclear as written, and the others are not needed beside Chapter 9.

rows.item: Idiom 52 of her list: Kick the bucket
rows.note: Used only as an informal, humorous way to say ‘die’ (beside die and pass away); it is also in Samiuallah’s notes.

rows.item: Idioms 53–58 of her list: Bought the farm; Pay through the nose; Take a powder; The icing on the cake; Soft-peddle; Fell off the deep end
rows.note: Mostly American slang, and ‘Fell off the deep end’ is unclear as written.

rows.item: Idioms 59–62 of her list: Put my cards on the table; Wear your heart on your sleeve; Put that in your pipe and smoke it; How the cookie crumbles
rows.note: Informal or American, and not needed beside the common idioms in Chapter 9.

rows.item: Maybe in a future version, a chapter on the common mistakes students fall into, with tips to avoid them
